Posted February 10, 2000
(MarijuanaNews note: This short article is one of the most damning that I have seen. It describes both the ultimate futility of the " drug war " -- but -- more importantly -- it details the horrible havoc that is being inflicted on our poor neighbors by our insane policies. Nonetheless, the Czar laughs at the damage done.)

February 10, 2000

Traffickers Moving Back to Caribbean -- US Drug Czar

By Michael Christie

MEXICO CITY (Reuters) - Latin America's drug cartels are switching their smuggling routes back through the Caribbean as Mexico tightens the screws in the Pacific, the U.S. anti-drug czar said.

The White House's chief anti-drug policymaker, Barry McCaffrey, who ends a two-day tour of Mexico Thursday, told U.S. reporters that Panama in particular faced a full-scale assault from narcotics traffickers since last December's handover of the Panama Canal.

" They're switching back. There's a lot more now showing up in the Haiti, Dom Rep (Dominican Republic), Jamaica axis. Haiti is the problem,'' McCaffrey said in a briefing in the U.S. ambassador's residence in Mexico City Wednesday night.

" And then I think a huge problem that's going to change rapidly is Panama. I think it's a target. These criminal organizations are pretty quick to respond.''

The United States completed its pullout from Panama in December under the terms of a 1977 treaty and handed over control of the canal after an almost century-long presence.

U.S. military bases in Panama, such as Howard Air Force Base, had become the hub of U.S. counter-narcotics surveillance and interdiction efforts in South America to stop the flow of cocaine from Colombia, Peru and Bolivia.

The U.S. anti-drugs command center was moved to Key West,

while Airborne warning and control systems (AWACS) aircraft now operate from Florida and Honduras, and F-16 jets and P-3 Orion naval patrols fly out of Curacao and Aruba in the Caribbean.

McCaffrey, in Mexico on a two-day tour of anti-drug operations in southern Mexican states and for talks with government officials, said Panama was trying to put together a defense capability but the cartels were bound to put it to the test.

" We're going to see a lot of stuff coming off the ferries (from neighboring Colombia), every flight out of Colombia ... that lands at Panama is going to have drugs on it. Every flight into Haiti has drugs on it,'' he said.

McCaffrey said that while the drug flows were changing, the Eastern Pacific remained the No. 1 smuggling route.

The Mexican Navy, often assisted by U.S. Coast Guard vessels, has increased its patrols in the Pacific and in recent months has seized at least three huge shipments of cocaine -- from three to 10 metric tons -- off Mexican fishing boats.

" The Mexican Navy and the Coast Guard aren't doing too badly. We still have some holes out in the Eastern Pacific that we're working on,'' McCaffrey said.

The retired four star general said Mexico's fight to cut down on cocaine smuggling through its territory and on local marijuana and heroin production was bearing fruit.

(MarijuanaNews note: As usual, the real emphasis is on marijuana, the easiest target.)

He said 55 percent of the cocaine consumed in the United States now came across the 2,100-mile (3,000-km) Mexican-U.S. border. A few years ago, U.S. officials estimated two-thirds of the cocaine sold in the United States passed through Mexico.

McCaffrey said eradication efforts, and to some extent drought in southern Mexican states, had cut annual Mexican heroin production to four metric tons from six metric tons previously. Marijuana production had also fallen.

A continuing problem was corruption, with low-paid and ill-trained state police forces unable to confront the might and the wealth of the powerful and violent drug cartels.

" The single most overwhelming threat of the drug organizations in my view is corruption,'' he said, adding the level of violence " is almost unbelievable. Every judge, every cop on a daily basis is facing these levels of violence.''

(MarijuanaNews note: Is this corruption? It sounds more like extortion to me, rather like what we do to the countries. The cartels threaten to kill the individuals. DEAland threatens to destroy the whole country. After all, DEAland invaded Panama, ostensibly to stop drug trafficking. In the process, we killed thousands of innocent Panamanians, and drug trafficking and money laundering is more wide-spread than ever.)

Added to the threat of assassination, was the cartels' ability to offer huge bribes.

McCaffrey said he has heard of a criminal organization offering an official $60 million.

``I told these guys (the Mexicans) ... you know, that's getting close to my price,'' McCaffrey joked.

(MarijuanaNews note: His " joke " is based on a probably apocryphal story about Lincoln. Lincoln is said to have politely refused a bribe, until after the offer was increased several times. Then he threw the would-be briber out bodily, explaining his anger by saying that the offer was getting too " close to his price. "

McCaffrey has sold his soul for a lot less
